item.title: [si.com] MLB Postseason Power Rankings: Strength and Weaknesses for Every Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Karl Rasmussen
item.description: The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series. The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. item.content:encoded:
The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series.
The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team to ever make the playoffs in a 162-game season, sneaking in and winning the division with just an 81–81 record.
Fans won’t have to wait long for postseason to get underway, with the Wild Card series set to begin on Tuesday. But before the action gets going, we’re going to do a final power ranking, assessing where all 12 teams sit and detailing their biggest strength and weakness.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching, lineup
Biggest weakness: Bullpen
The Dodgers may be the No. 2 seed in the National League, but they’re built to win in October. It’s hard to determine what’s a greater strength between their loaded starting rotation or their star-studded lineup. There’s no weaknesses in their rotation, with All-Star caliber pitchers available to take the mound every night, even with Shohei Ohtani restricted to DH duties. There isn’t a team in MLB with more postseason experience than Los Angeles, who have won back-to-back World Series with this core. During the regular season, the Dodgers had MLB’s second-highest OPS (.762) and fourth-best ERA (3.55). If there’s any way to beat them it’s by getting after a bullpen that has been inconsistent throughout the season, though it’s still a top-10 unit. Injuries have plagued their relief pitching corps, however, with the likes of Blake Treinen, Edgardo Henriquez and Will Klein all currently on IL.
2. Milwaukee Brewers
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Brewers’ rotation, headlined by NL Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski, has been one of MLB’s best, and it’s helped the team secure the league’s best regular-season record. The starting rotation owns MLB’s fifth-best ERA (3.65) and their bullpen has been equally impressive, ranking third in MLB with a 3.40 ERA. Milwaukee has scored the second-most runs in the league this season (832), as their small-ball approach has worked wonders for them. But in October, when a single swing of the bat can dramatically change a team’s fortunes and rallies are harder to come by, they might not have the power hitters capable of providing that big home run swing. The Brewers didn’t have a single 30-home run hitter this season and had just three everyday starters with a slugging percentage above .450.
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Bottom-third of the lineup
The Rays had the best record in the American League this season, largely thanks to their pitching. The starting rotation has been excellent, ranking third in MLB with a 3.51 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has quietly been one of MLB’s best arms, and Freddy Peralta has begun to rediscover his previous form after a rough go with the Mets and a shaky start on the mound in Tampa. Much like the Brewers, the Rays primarily utilize a small-ball approach offensively. The Rays hit the ninth-fewest home runs in MLB this year, and despite rostering some elite hitters such as Junior Caminero and Yandy Diaz, they haven’t received much production out of the bottom third of their lineup, which is their biggest weakness with the postseason looming.
4. Atlanta Braves
Biggest strength: Deep lineup
Biggest weakness: Plate discipline, low on-base rates
The Braves are another team with an abundance of postseason experience in the lineup. They have several players that can turn a game on its head with one swing of the bat, and had five 20-plus home run hitters during the regular season in Matt Olson, Michael Harris, Drake Baldwin, Ozzie Albies and Ronald Acuña Jr. Although the lineup is flush with talent, the group has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone, and they don’t draw walks at a high rate. The Braves ranked 28th in MLB in on-base percentage (.309) during the regular season, often opting for an aggressive approach at the plate rather than a patient one. That could prove costly in October against some of the best pitchers in the sport, where slowing the game down and getting runners on base by any means necessary will be crucial.
5. New York Yankees
Biggest strength: Elite pitching rotation
Biggest weakness: Offense (without Aaron Judge), high strikeout rates
Yankees starting pitchers led MLB with a 3.30 ERA this season, and they’ll have one of the best rotations in the postseason with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon set to take the mound in October. The bullpen has been a bit inconsistent, but they should be able to ride their starting rotation deep into games. The biggest weakness for the Yankees is their lineup, particularly without Aaron Judge in the mix. New York had the sixth-most strikeouts this season and were tied for 11th in MLB with a .720 OPS. With Judge out of the lineup, however, their OPS falls to a .690 mark, which would be 29th in MLB.
6. San Diego Padres
Biggest strength: Elite bullpen
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Padres’ bullpen has been as reliable as they come this season, and the team flexes multiple elite relievers who they can reliably turn the ball over to in the later innings in Mason Miller, Yuki Matsui and Adrian Morejon, among others. San Diego has shaken off a slow start to the year and are playing at an extremely high level heading into the postseason. The offense is alive again after a dreadful first couple of months of the season, with players like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill having been among MLB’s best second-half performers at the plate. The starting pitching will be the x-factor in October, however. With Casey Mize landing on the IL, their options in the rotation are even thinner. Remaining competitive within the first six innings will be crucial for the Padres, whose starting pitchers rank 21st in MLB with a 4.42 ERA this year.
7. Chicago Cubs
Biggest strength: Dominant lineup
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Cubs have had MLB’s best offense this season, leading the league in OPS (.767), walks (674), runs scored (850) and slugging percentage (.428). They’ve been particularly elite since the All-Star break, logging a .797 OPS in their last 66 games. With Pete Crow-Armstrong playing at an MVP level and Alex Bregman having enjoyed a monster second half, the Cubs’ offense will be tough to shut down in October. Of course, they’ll need their pitching to live up to their end of the bargain, which it’s struggled to do this season. Chicago’s starting pitching has been disappointing and plagued by injuries. The starting rotation ranks 18th in MLB with a 4.27 ERA this year and have surrendered the third-most home runs (142).
8. Boston Red Sox
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Inconsistent offense
The Red Sox’s pitching as a whole has been excellent. Boston’s bullpen owns a league-best 3.00 ERA this season, and no group of relievers in MLB has surrendered fewer home runs (55). Their starters have been great, too, ranking eighth in the league with a 3.92 ERA, and they boast a solid mix of veterans (Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez) and young, emerging starters (Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett). Offensively, however, the Red Sox have been prone to spells of inconsistency. They started the season ice cold before enjoying a scalding hot summer streak, but they’ve come crashing back down to earth in the final month of the season. The Red Sox rank dead last in MLB in OPS (.651) throughout the month of September, and they’re batting a league-worst .219 in that span.
9. Cleveland Guardians
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Guardians starting pitching has been a top-10 unit this season, ranking ninth in ERA (3.93) and fifth in strikeouts (878). Parker Messick has been superb in his first full season in MLB, and Gavin Williams has emerged as one of the league’s best strikeout pitchers. Cleveland will feel confident with those two spearheading the rotation, but they may struggle to get the run support required to take advantage of their quality starters. The Guardians rank 24th in MLB with 678 runs scored, 26th in OPS (.696) and 27th in home runs (162) this season. If they can’t come up with some big at-bats, it won’t matter how effective their pitching is in October.
10. Philadelphia Phillies
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Defense, bullpen
The Phillies have one of the best starting rotations in MLB, but they’ve been plagued by some underperforming position players and a lackluster bullpen. There’s arguably no better trio of starters in MLB than Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesús Luzardo. The team’s starting rotation ranks seventh in the league with a 3.80 ERA, but their bullpen ranks 21st in ERA (4.43). Defensively, the Phillies have been atrocious, too. Only the Athletics have fewer defensive runs saved than the Phillies’ -43, according to the Fielding Bible, and the infield has been a serious concern, with Trea Turner, Bryce Harper and Alec Bohm all ranking among the bottom 26 defensive players (of 270 qualified players) in MLB in terms of outs above average, per Statcast. Defensive shortcomings and mishaps could prove highly costly in October, and that’s an area that’s plagued Philadelphia all season.
11. Chicago White Sox
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The White Sox have a potent lineup and are the only team in MLB that have three players who hit 30 or more home runs in Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery. Chicago hit the fifth-most home runs this season (211) and scored the fifth-most runs (776). While the offense is among the league’s best in terms of power, the White Sox starting pitching is a serious concern. The starting rotation posted a season ERA of 4.60 (fourth-worst in MLB), a 1.34 WHIP (sixth-worst in MLB) and recorded the third-fewest strikeouts of any starting rotation in the league. Chicago’s starters also threw the fewest innings in MLB this season, often struggling to get deep into games before the baton was passed to the bullpen. If the starting rotation can’t keep runs off the board, it might not matter how explosive their lineup can be.
12. Houston Astros
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
Yordan Alvarez is likely to win the AL MVP, and he’s the type of hitter teams will not be eager to pitch to in October. No team in MLB hit more home runs than the Astros, who hit 226. In addition to Alvarez’s 42, Houston had four other players with 20-plus homers, including Christian Walker (29), Isaac Paredes (25), Jeremy Peña (22) and Cam Smith (21). They don’t have much to worry about offensively, but their lineup will need to produce in order to ease the burden on their starting rotation, which has largely struggled this year. Hunter Brown remains a reliable ace, but beyond him there’s a lack of experience and talent within the rotation. Astros starters ranked 27th in MLB with a 4.81 ERA and 1.40 WHIP, both of which were the worst among all teams that qualified for the postseason, and they walked the most batters in MLB this season. If the lineup can’t make up for the rotation’s shortcomings, it could be a short postseason stint for Houston this year.
Karl Rasmussen is a staff writer for Sports Illustrated. A University of Oregon alum who joined SI in February 2023, his work has appeared on 12up and ClutchPoints. Rasmussen is a loyal Tottenham, Jets, Yankees and Ducks fan.
Follow Karlras920

item.title: [CBS Sports] Pete Crow-Armstrong just wrapped up one of the best Cubs seasons ever, and he's not done yet

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong was in a sort of mini-funk. The All-Star center fielder had gone 3 for his previous 20 with seven strikeouts and no extra-base hits and the Cubs were headed into a mid-September three-game series against the eventual NL East champion Braves. He was still the overwhelming favorite to win the National League MVP, but things hadn't been going right.
He popped out in foul territory in his first at-bat. Next time up, PCA sent a rocket double down the right-field line. And it was, as they say, on. He finished the game with four hits, including a home run, and four RBI. Two nights later, he went 3 for 4 with a triple and two home runs. In a single series against a playoff team, he had one four-hit game and another 11-base game.
"When he hit the second homer, Alex Bregman was standing next to me," Cubs manager Craig Counsell said after the two-home run game (via MLB.com). "I said, 'Alex, we don't get to see things like this.' You spend your whole life in baseball and you just don't see this happen on a baseball field. You're grateful to be a part of it.
"You're grateful to see things like this. And you're grateful that the fans get to see a season like this, because they're going to talk about it. They're going to tell their kids about it. They're going to tell their grandkids about seasons like this."
Bregman has seen plenty of elite-level play, too. The two-time World Series champion and four-time pennant winner played with 2017 American League MVP José Altuve and finished second himself in 2019. He was in the same division as Mike Trout for nine years. And Counsell is telling him about how special this is?
Counsell would know, too. As a player, he won the World Series with the 1997 Marlins and 2001 Diamondbacks. He was teammates with Ryan Braun during his 2011 MVP campaign and came up with the Rockies in the '90s while Larry Walker was in his prime. He also managed Christian Yelich during his MVP season in 2018.
And still, he sees something special in Crow-Armstrong.
The younger guys are taking notice, too.
"As far as the seasons I've seen in my experience in professional baseball, this is the best," Cubs utility infielder Matt Shaw told CBS Sports. "I don't think I've seen anything that even compares."
Crow-Armstrong finished his magical 2026 season on Sunday when he was removed for a pinch runner after singling to start the game. The final line: .280/.372/.570 (155 OPS+) with 31 doubles, eight triples, 45 home runs, 107 RBI, 119 runs, 41 steals, 9.8 bWAR, 10.6 fWAR and some of the best defensive stats in baseball. He was the seventh player in MLB history to reach the .
It was one of the very best individual seasons in Cubs history.
The origin story
Through June 24, 2021, the Cubs were sitting in a first-place tie thanks to a roster largely made up of their 2016 World Series heroes. After throwing a combined no-hitter in Dodger Stadium, the Cubs proceeded to lose three straight games. They headed to Milwaukee on June 28 to start a three-game series. They were outscored 41-8 in a Brewers sweep, with Counsell at the helm as Milwaukee's skipper.
This was the start of the end for that 2021 Cubs team, which completely fell apart and eventually saw the front office tear up the 2016 nucleus and move on. Kris Bryant and Anthony Rizzo were traded, as was fan favorite Javier Báez to the Mets in a deal that also included pitcher Trevor Williams. In return came a 19-year-old kid named Pete Crow-Armstrong.
Crow-Armstrong wasn't some obscure tack-on on whom the Cubs got lucky. He had been drafted No. 19 out of high school the year prior. His upside was well known.
Still, he had only six games of professional experience before falling injured that season. There was upside to dream on, but also a lot of unknown.
PCA debuted late in 2023 and looked overmatched at the plate, going 0 for 14 with seven strikeouts. Still, heading into 2024, he was a consensus top-20 prospect in all of baseball. The projections were that he'd be elite in center field, elite on the bases and had a decent chance to become a good hitter. Maybe something like a .275 average, .340 on-base percentage and 15-20 homers would become a normal season.
He showed flashes on offense in 2024, especially given that he was only 22 years old, but failed to live up to expectations.
Then there was the first-half breakout in 2025, followed by a disaster of a second half at the plate. The eye test said he was a totally different hitter. The splits line up:
1st half: .265/.302/.544
2nd half: .216/.262/.372
The poor plate performance carried over into 2026. He was only hitting .224/.314/.362 through May 29. And then, amid "overrated" chants from Cardinals fans in St. Louis, he went deep and took off for the rest of the season.
From that game through the end of the season, Crow-Armstrong hit .308 with an OBP above .400, slugged nearly .700 and clubbed 39 home runs in 104 games. One of the biggest differences has been his grasp of the strike zone, cutting down on swinging at bad pitches and doing damage on strikes.
Sure enough, his walk rate rose from 4.5% last season to 11.4% this year. He reduced the rate at which he swung at pitches outside the strike zone by more than 7 points. He swung roughly 10% less overall. His hard-hit percentage went from 41.6 to 48.5. Again, the formula: Swing less, swing at fewer bad pitches, do more damage when you do swing.
It sounds simple, but it's a difficult adjustment at the big-league level, and many young players never pull it off. PCA did it at age 24 and turned into one of the best players in baseball.
"Absolutely," Crow-Armstrong told CBS Sports when asked if he thought this type of season was possible. "That's what I work for."
A jaw-dropping 2026 season
Crow-Armstrong's 40-40 season made him just the seventh player ever to pull off the feat. He had seven four-hit games this season, leading the majors (Jackson Chourio was second with six).
He led the majors in runs scored. He was sixth in hits and tied for fifth in triples. He tied former Cubs (and current Phillies) slugger Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead in home runs. He tied for fourth in steals. He led a handful of defensive metrics.
And, despite being a primary leadoff man, PCA finished fourth in the majors in RBI.
The list of primary leadoff men who topped 100 RBI in a season is awfully short. PCA didn't hit leadoff all season, but he racked up 83 RBI in only 107 games from that position. Shohei Ohtani's 84 in 90 games is one of the few seasons with more bulk at a higher rate per game. The record is 107 from Mookie Betts in 2023, and that was in 151 games from the leadoff spot. Still, to finish fourth in RBI despite leading off over 100 times is ridiculous.
Remember that 11-base game? He reached 10 total bases six times this season, tying the MLB record along with 2019 Nelson Cruz (only 1997 Larry Walker, 1940 Johnny Mize and 1933 Jimmie Foxx even had five such games in a season).
How about if we cherry-pick the numbers and go with 45 home runs, eight triples and 30 doubles in a season? Crow-Armstrong did that this year. The others who have done so? Babe Ruth (twice), Lou Gehrig (twice), Jimmie Foxx (three times), Joe DiMaggio and Eddie Mathews. That's it. Mathews and PCA are the only two to get there since integration, and PCA is the only player since 1953.
And even as the bat has leveled up, the defense and baserunning haven't lagged behind at all. He's become an all-around force, and that shows up in WAR. Crow-Armstrong led the majors in both major versions of WAR. In FanGraphs' metric, it wasn't even remotely close: Bobby Witt Jr. finished second among position players at 6.9. PCA had 10.6.
In fact, if we stick with FanGraphs' WAR, the only seasons higher this century than PCA's 2026 are three Barry Bonds seasons and two Aaron Judge seasons. That's it. He's topped the best career mark posted by Albert Pujols, Alex Rodriguez, Mike Trout, Miguel Cabrera, Mookie Betts, Ronald Acuña Jr., Shohei Ohtani and, well, everyone else but Bonds and Judge.
The Cubs have been around since 1876. The only player to post a higher fWAR in a season in franchise history than PCA did this season was Rogers Hornsby in 1929. Yes, this Pete Crow-Armstrong season rated higher via this metric than anything from Ernie Banks, Ron Santo, Billy Williams, Ryne Sandberg and Sammy Sosa.
Again, the defensive and baserunning chops were always going to be there. It's the offensive strides that made him special this season.
What's next?
"That'll be a never-ending process," Crow-Armstrong told CBS Sports earlier this month when asked what improvements his game needs. "I view it as, if I can do this now, I still carry the belief that I have more in me and, yeah, there's always going to be things I can get better at and I would hope that's how my career goes. That would be a very lucky way to be able to experience this game -- just experiencing yourself growing every year. That's really what I've come to notice the most this year is that I've been very aware of growth."
For Crow-Armstrong, everything is about the greater goal: winning, and winning as a team.
"We're here to win baseball games, we're not here to show up and reach individual milestones," he said. "Those just happen by playing good baseball."
He's done plenty of that in 2026. Now the focus will be on helping the Cubs to their first deep playoff run since 2017.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

29 Sep 2026, 06:49 GMT+10

(Photo credit: David Frerker)
The Chicago Cubs eliminated the San Diego Padres from the postseason a year ago and then scored 55 runs while going 5-1 against them this season.
But nobody is expecting that type of one-sided matchup to continue as the Padres are hotter than lava entering Tuesday night's National League wild-card series opener against visiting Chicago.
The Padres (91-71) are a sizzling 41-18 since July 24, transforming a bumbling campaign into a third straight postseason berth, a first in franchise history.
In the final days of the season, San Diego overtook the Cubs (89-73) to secure the No. 4 seed, granting the Padres home-field advantage in the best-of-three series. Chicago, the No. 5 seed, hosted at Wrigley Field last season and beat the Padres in three games in the wild-card round.
Playing the series at pitcher-friendly Petco Park could lessen the Cubs' offensive advantage. Chicago led the majors with 850 runs this season, while the Padres scored 722.
The Cubs feature leading NL MVP candidate Pete Crow-Armstrong, who recorded a 40-40 season by tying for the major league lead with 45 homers and adding 41 steals. He also led the majors with 84 extra-base hits and 119 runs.
Crow-Armstrong batted .364 (8-for-22) with four homers and 10 RBIs against San Diego this season.
'I'm looking forward to playing a really good ballclub and getting another crack at them and starting this playoffs off on a high note,' Crow-Armstrong said Monday.
San Diego's Manny Machado batted a career-low .217 but smacked 30 homers, marking the eighth time in his career he has hit at least that many.
More important to the Padres is Fernando Tatis Jr., who didn't hit his first homer until May 30 and had just five at the All-Star break. He hit 20 blasts after the break and was a major catalyst for the team's torrid 59-game finish.
'It's a baseball game. We have to get 27 outs and hopefully be the last team standing,' Machado said.
Right-hander Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA) will start for the Padres against Cubs left-hander Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91).
King has made two career postseason starts, both in 2024 for the Padres. The most memorable one came in Game 1 of the wild-card series against the Atlanta Braves when he tossed seven shutout innings and struck out 12.
King gave up one hit and struck out three in one inning of relief against the Cubs in the 2025 postseason series, his lone appearance against them with the Padres. He also twice faced Chicago in relief when he was with the New York Yankees.
'Very professional lineup,' King said of the Cubs. 'They were first in runs this year and it shows. I keep saying that when the pitcher executes, we have the upper hand so I have to make sure I am executing throughout and putting up as many zeroes as I can.'
Chicago's Alex Bregman is 7-for-8 with two doubles against King.
Bregman surged over the final two months, delivering 17 homers and 46 RBIs to get his season outputs to 28 and 93, respectively.
Bregman is playing with multiple fractures in his left cheek after getting hit by a foul ball off the bat of teammate Michael Busch during a game on Sept. 20.
Boyd, 35, is 0-1 with a 1.66 ERA in seven playoff appearances (six starts). He was 0-1 with a 2.79 ERA in three starts for Chicago last postseason and gave up one run and four hits over 4 1/3 innings when the Cubs beat the Padres in Game 1 of last year's wild-card series.
'The Padres are one of the hottest teams in baseball the past few weeks,' Boyd said. 'That's not surprising. We've seen them firsthand -- this year, last year. I always firmly believe that it's more about what's in this clubhouse and less about what's on the other side. Take care of your business.'
Boyd is 2-1 with a 4.43 ERA in four regular-season outings against San Diego. Machado is 9-for-20 (.450) with a homer and four doubles against Boyd.
The winner of this series faces the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Division Series.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — The Chicago Cubs are again turning to left-hander Matthew Boyd to begin their postseason.
Boyd, who got the Game 1 start in last year’s wild-card series against the San Diego Padres, will again get the ball when the Cubs open their rematch Tuesday, this time at Petco Park. The Cubs also could have started right-hander Kevin Gausman but opted for the lefty. Boyd held the Padres to one run in 4 1/3 innings in Game 1 last season at Wrigley Field.
“The first two months of the season were certainly interrupted and not smooth, but since then he’s gotten into a routine and consistency, that is what I think Matthew offers,” manager Craig Counsell said Monday after their team workout. “Playoff starts are a challenge. Matthew’s experienced in that and had good experiences last year with it for us and look for him to do the same tomorrow.”
Since returning from meniscus surgery June 25, Boyd posted a 3.42 ERA in his final 17 starts, allowing three earned runs or fewer in 12 of those outings.
Counsell didn’t provide specifics on who could start Games 2 or 3, the latter if necessary Thursday. Gausman is expected to pitch at some point in the series. His left shoulder injury sustained in his final regular-season start Wednesday created some uncertainty about whether he would be available this playoff round. The Cubs feel Gausman’s shoulder is trending well but isn’t fully in the clear, making a Tuesday start not a realistic option.
The Cubs are expected to carry 12 pitchers on their wild-card roster. Left-hander Shota Imanaga is also expected to factor into the Cubs’ pitching plans this series, though Counsell cautioned he didn’t know whether that would be as a starter or a reliever. Right-hander Clay Holmes wasn’t at his best down the stretch, but the Cubs anticipate him providing bulk in some capacity this series, whether that’s in a start or multiple innings out of the bullpen.
The best-of-three series allows Counsell to fully deploy all his pitchers as needed, whether it’s using starters out of the bullpen for multiple frames or even one-inning appearances. The Cubs will seek the best matchups and pockets of hitters for their pitchers to face.
“I look at these games kind of in this context that we’re talking about the urgency is you have 27 outs, we’ve got to figure out how to get 27 outs,” Counsell said. “The order that that happens — starter, reliever, closer, setup man — those words don’t matter. We’re just trying to get 27 outs.”
The Cubs’ pitching plans beyond Game 1 will be dictated by whether they win or lose the opener. It’ll be all hands on deck Wednesday for Game 2 if they don’t pull out the win Tuesday.
“It doesn’t matter how anything happens tomorrow, like aesthetically, it just matters that we win, that’s the bottom line,” Counsell said. “Because we’ve got to win two games in the next three days and so how anybody does, how anything happens, it doesn’t matter. You’ve got to win the game. And I think you probably lean more on the process over 162 games because you have to. But when you get to a two-out-of-three series to play the next game, your thoughts have to change a little bit.”
In a rematch of last year’s wild-card matchup, a venue change presents an added challenge for the Cubs against a Padres team with one of the best home records in baseball — 51-30 at Petco Park this year compared to 40-41 on the road.
The Cubs haven’t decided yet whether Alex Bregman is feeling well enough to start at third base or if they keep using him as the designated hitter to reduce the risk as he continues to play with multiple facial fractures. He took grounders at third base during live batting practice Monday, an encouraging development.
Bregman’s quick return gives the Cubs’ lineup added juice.
“I definitely think that fires you up,” Pete Crow-Armstrong said Monday. “Knowing him and how wonderfully crazed he is just about his work and how much he loves the game, not really surprising. Not to put a damper on how cool it is that he is coming back after eight facial fractures and whatnot, like, I’m just not surprised. He lives for this kind of baseball.”

item.title: [chicago.suntimes.com] These four things could make the difference in Cubs’ wild-card playoff series vs. Padres

item.description: SAN DIEGO — The playoffs have arrived. item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — The playoffs have arrived.
The Cubs have been building to this all season long, eyeing a run deep into October.
‘‘This group is ready,’’ catcher Carson Kelly said Sunday. ‘‘It’s been a long year. We’ve had our ups and downs. But what this group does really well is we come prepared every single day.’’
To get to where they want to go, the Cubs first need to get past the Padres, their opponent in a best-of-three wild-card series.
Here’s what could make the difference:
Pete Crow-Armstrong
Crow-Armstrong has been the best player in baseball this season and soon will have an MVP award on his mantel to show for it.
But the individual accolades have meant little to Crow-Armstrong, given that he’s focused on team goals. The chase for the biggest of those — a World Series title — starts now.
It’s a team sport, and everyone will have to do their job for the Cubs to win. But if you’re going to talk about the impact one player can make, Crow-Armstrong can make more than just about anyone else in the playoffs.
‘‘We’re fortunate we get to see it in person every single day,’’ Kelly said. ‘‘There are a lot of times where we’ll look at each other and say, ‘Oh, my gosh, did that really just happen?’
‘‘Sometimes he gets up there, and you’re like, ‘OK, Pete’s going to hit a homer.’ He hits it, and you’re like, ‘What?’ Or running a ball down in the gap. Stealing a base, stealing second and third. You’re like, ‘This guy, he does it all.’ ’’
Alex Bregman
A week ago, the Cubs didn’t know what Bregman would be able to give them, if anything, in the postseason after taking a foul ball off his face.
But not only are they able to include Bregman in their playoff plans, they can count him as a
centerpiece.
A week removed from his freak injury, Bregman homered twice as part of a four-hit Sunday.
San Diego. Drink it in. It always goes down smooth. Just like these couple two tree things about the Cubs the night before the playoffs start. @suntimes_sports @Suntimes pic.twitter.com/2j45VXUP43
— Vinnie Duber (@VinnieDuber) September 29, 2026
Bregman got back to being Bregman in a hurry, and that’s a big deal. The Cubs signed him to a five-year, $175 million free-agent deal in part to be a force in October, where he’s one of the most accomplished postseason hitters of all time.
And showing some Chicago toughness helps, too.
‘‘It fires you up,’’ Crow-Armstrong said Monday. ‘‘Knowing him and how wonderfully crazed he is about his work and how much he loves the game, it’s not really surprising. Not to put a damper on how cool it is, him coming back after eight facial fractures and whatnot, I’m just not that surprised. He lives for this kind of baseball.
‘‘Most important, I’m glad he’s healthy enough to do what he loves. But selfishly, I’m pumped that he’s going to be in our lineup for these important games. Simply put, Alex Bregman makes our lineup better, so it’s huge he’s getting himself game-ready.’’
The bullpen
It wasn’t long ago that the Cubs’ bullpen was in disarray.
But things have stabilized a bit, with manager Craig Counsell leaning on right-handers Ryan Zeferjahn (1.13 ERA in his last nine outings) and Daniel Palencia (eight scoreless appearances in a row) to great effect.
Palencia is looking more like the guy who dazzled last season, and Zeferjahn is looking more like the guy the Cubs thought they landed in a deadline deal.
‘‘He’s had some good outings lately,’’ Counsell said of Zeferjahn. ‘‘I feel great about him. He’s going to pitch. He’s going to be a major part of this at the end here.’’
The Cubs don’t necessarily have a designated closer, not that they see that as a problem, given Counsell’s ‘‘out-getters’’ mantra. But should any fans fret that is the team’s Achilles’ heel, maybe Zeferjahn can put their minds at ease.
‘‘There’s ups and downs, and I rode that ‘down’ for a little bit,’’ Zeferjahn said. ‘‘But I’ve been working my way back up. . . . Hopefully, I’m riding an all-time high here going into the playoffs.’’
The conditions
The Cubs led baseball in runs scored this season, but the bats didn’t look great last week, averaging just two runs a game.
But heading to San Diego could have its advantages.
Kelly compared trying to hit at Wrigley Field and Fenway Park last week — they scored nine total runs in five games at the cold, windy venues — “like you’re hitting into a fan.”
The Cubs moved indoors Sunday and scored six runs. That’s only one game, hardly an indicator of what’s to come. But not dealing with poor hitting conditions is one way to allow a capable Cubs lineup to flex its muscles.
The catch? They might have to get real muscly, as the Padres — quite used to hitting in nice weather — have been on a roll, with only one team in baseball (the Brewers) scoring more runs in September.

item.title: [bleedcubbieblue.com] The Short Porch and the Cubs have jet lag
item.dc:creator: Sara Sanchez
item.description: The end of the 2026 season has been a rocky road for the Chicago Cubs. September was one of two months that saw them post sub-.500 marks on the season with an 11-13 record. They finished exactly .500 in their last 10 games. They dropped two winnable games against the Red Sox and two winnable games against the Marlins. item.content:encoded:
The end of the 2026 season has been a rocky road for the Chicago Cubs. September was one of two months that saw them post sub-.500 marks on the season with an 11-13 record. They finished exactly .500 in their last 10 games. They dropped two winnable games against the Red Sox and two winnable games against the Marlins. It felt like they might be limping into the Postseason even before star third baseman Alex Bregman took a foul ball to the face, resulting in multiple fractures and multiple missed games for one of the Cubs best hitters in the second half.
Oh, you thought that was the bad news? There’s more! While that string of bad luck alone would have (probably) played the Cubs out of hosting a Wild Card Series at the Friendly Confines of Wrigley Field, Mother Nature wanted to get in on the action too. A freak September nor’easter descended upon Boston in the waning days of the 2026 season and MLB’s “solution” to this was the following itinerary for the Chicago Cubs:
- Thursday, Sept. 24: Day game at Wrigley, fly to Boston
- Friday, Sept. 25: Doubleheader in Boston, fly to Tampa
- Saturday, Sept. 26: Impromptu off day in Florida!
- Sunday, Sept. 27: Play one game in Tropicana Field to finish the season for #reasons, fly to San Diego
- Monday, Sept. 28: Workout day for the Wild Card Series
- Tuesday, Sept. 29: Begin best of three Wild Card Series in San Diego. First pitch scheduled at 10PM Eastern Time
It’s not particularly becoming in baseball to complain about certain things. After all, both teams have the same weather, the same umpires, the same roster rules and restrictions. They don’t have the same talent, but they did that to themselves and frankly, any difference in injury risk is likely a result of player decisions and tradeoffs someone made along the way as well. But this isn’t so much complaining as observing that MLB has chosen to deal the Cubs an absolutely brutal hand en route to the Postseason, which will kick off for them in San Diego tomorrow.
The question is, how will they handle it? You don’t have to look further than Bregman for answers. Bregman DH’d against the Red Sox and while it took a few at bats to get his timing back, he eventually did this [VIDEO].
It’s obviously an incorrect inference to suggest that two swings of the bat can salvage a downturn that likely reflects a depleted bullpen pitching on fumes. That said, stranger things have happened in this season that saw the Cubs win 10 games in a row twice and lose 10 straight in another stretch. It feels like the deck is stacked against the Cubs, but this isn’t really a team that has thrown in the towel or given up at any sign of adversity this season.
This team lost Cade Horton, Justin Steele had a setback, Ben Brown emerged as a legit TOR starter before being lost for the season and they kept winning anyway. Pete Crow-Armstrong looked like he was struggling early, only to emerge as the first 40-40 man in franchise history and the likely NL MVP. Alex Bregman hitting home runs with a broken face might just be the 2026 iteration of the Cubs channeling the 2016 team’s “We Never Quit.”
There’s no such thing as an easy road to a championship. The Cubs road continues tomorrow at Petco Park, and I doubt they’ll let something as trivial as jet lag define their season.

item.title: [fansided.com] Evaluating the Hall of Fame trajectories of Shohei Ohtani and MLB’s postseason stars
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman

item.content:encoded:
Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. The likes of Bryce Harper, Justin Verlander, and Mike Trout all were locks, and rightfully so.
But as the MLB playoffs prepare to kick off, Verlander and Trout are once again sitting at home. Harper and the Phillies survived a near-collapse to secure a Wild Card seed, and he’s one of many postseason participants who could — and in his case, should — find themselves in the Hall of Fame one day.
Besides the obvious counting stats, what makes a Hall of Famer? As we’ve previously noted, baseball fans have recently accepted 40 bWAR as the standard for a remarkable career. Immaculate Grid is to thank on that front, even if there are players who have cleared that mark but don’t feel like Hall of Famers. Astros shortstop Carlos Correa, who is injured but has a 47.1 bWAR, is a perfect example, and he didn’t crack our list.
Instead, let’s turn our attention to someone who may very well become the second unanimous electee when his time comes.
Honorable mention: The Shohei Ohtani tier
Barring any unprecedented rule changes, Hall of Fame candidates must have 10 full seasons worth of experience for eligibility. That means Shohei Ohtani would technically be ineligible if he retired tomorrow, so he won’t land in the “lock” tier.
But Ohtani has always been a unicorn, so him having his own category makes all too much sense. We can all agree that, at this time next year, Ohtani should be a lock on that list.
Not yet eligible, but…
These guys don’t get their own table, but we wanted to address their situations ahead of the playoffs.
- Aroldis Chapman, P, Boston Red Sox: Off the numbers alone, Chapman and his 402 saves (ninth all-time) likely warrant induction. However, he also served a 30-game suspension in 2016 for violating the league’s domestic violence policy. It’s difficult to envision him earning the 75 percent required for election. Recent voting trends don’t work in favor of those who have been suspended for performance-enhancing drugs (more on that soon) or off-field incidents.
- Cam Schlittler, SP, New York Yankees and Jacob Misirowski, SP, Milwaukee Brewers: We’re lumping these two together because both will be trending during the playoffs. Just because these two are likely to win their league’s respective Cy Young Awards doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed a spot in Cooperstown. Heck, we don’t even know if they’ll pitch long enough to appear on a ballot! But, you know how baseball fans are.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., 2B/RF, San Diego Padres: As things currently stand, Tatis has no chance of getting into the Hall of Fame. Voters have made it clear that those who serve PED-related suspensions, as Tatis did in 2022, aren’t welcome in Cooperstown unless they buy a ticket. That said, we’re including him here
- Tarik Skubal, SP, Los Angeles Dodgers: Skubal became the 23rd pitcher in MLB history to win multiple Cy Young Awards, which will appeal to voters who prefer the "dominant" peak. But we’d like to see at least two or three more years of him being at least above-average. He’s also only seven seasons in, so he has a lot of work left.
On pace to make it into Cooperstown
- Alex Bregman, Chicago Cubs - 48.9 bWAR
- Matt Olson, Atlanta Braves - 44.2 bWAR
- Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros - 30.5 bWAR
These three have team success, specifically at least one World Series ring, working in their favor. Alvarez is likely to win AL MVP, and the 29-year-old is young enough that clearing 40 bWAR shouldn’t be an issue so long as healthy.
Bregman turns 33 next March, and his bWAR is likely far greater than you’d have guessed. But is he truly on a Hall of Fame trajectory? He's nowhere close to 2,000 hits (1,411) or 300 home runs (237), both of which are vital numbers when playing the hot corner.
Consider, though, that Bregman has averaged 24 home runs, 84 RBIs, 32 doubles, and 4.6 bWAR over the last five years. He’s under contract through 2030, and exceeded all of those numbers (28 home runs, 93 RBIs, 33 doubles, and 5.8 bWAR) this season.
If Bregman were to continue averaging those numbers, he’d end the 2031 season with 333 home runs, roughly 2,200 hits, and 481 doubles. Oh, and his bWAR would be right around 72.0, so we imagine he’d be a first-ballot inductee.
Unfortunately for him and Olson, the possibility of a work stoppage could have a monumental impact on their final counting stats. Which leads us into…
Borderline veterans
- Giancarlo Stanton, New York Yankees - 47.0 bWAR
- Zack Wheeler, Philadelphia Phillies - 46.6 bWAR
- Gerrit Cole, SP, New York Yankees - 45.8 bWAR
- Christian Yelich, Milwaukee Brewers - 45.1 bWAR
- Xander Bogaerts, SS, San Diego Padres - 44.3 bWAR
- Max Fried, P, New York Yankees - 32.3 bWAR
- Kyle Schwarber, OF/DH, Philadelphia Phillies - 22.3 bWAR
Stanton and Schwarber’s cases are likely dependent on whether they surpass 500 home runs. The latter will enter next season at 385 homers, and he turns 34 in March. But the looming work stoppage could significantly affect his chances of reaching 400 anytime soon.
As for Stanton, multiple lower-body injuries limited him to three homers in 24 games. Although he has 466 career home runs, the 2017 NL MVP turns 37 in November and is a free agent after next year.
The only members of the 500-home run club who aren’t in the Hall of Fame are either ineligible or have ties to performance-enhancing drugs. It’d be pretty remarkable if Schwarber and Stanton both cleared the historic total yet fell short of Cooperstown.
Personally, Wheeler and Cole are probably the only ones who will have a legitimate Hall of Fame résumé when they become eligible. The rest of those guys are Hall of Very Good at best. Much like Skubal, we need two or three more elite seasons from Fried before we’d even consider voting for him.
Go ahead and make the Hall of Fame plaque
- Mookie Betts, Los Angeles Dodgers - 79.0 bWAR
- Freddie Freeman, Los Angeles Dodgers - 66.8 bWAR
- Paul Goldschmidt, New York Yankees - 65.1 bWAR
- Aaron Judge, New York Yankees - 64.2 bWAR
- Manny Machado, San Diego Padres - 63.3 bWAR
- Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves - 62.7 bWAR
- José Ramírez, Cleveland Guardians - 60.3 bWAR
- Bryce Harper, Philadelphia Phillies - 56.9 bWAR
- Jose Altuve, Houston Astros - 53.4 bWAR
Outside of Goldschmidt and Sale, none of these names are overly surprising. And no, the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal shouldn’t impact Altuve, especially not after Carlos Beltrán just entered the Hall of Fame.
Goldschmidt currently ranks 143rd on the all-time bWAR list, and only 31 men above him aren’t already enshrined. But of the 20 who are or were eligible, most came up short for PED or off-field reasons. The question then becomes whether he’s wearing a Diamondbacks or Cardinals cap, or if he opts for the blank hat.
Although Sale turns 38 next March, he has a lifetime 2.95 ERA and 2,779 strikeouts, putting him within range of reaching 3,000. There’s absolutely no reason why he shouldn’t be a first-ballot selection.
As for the rest? You know a Hall of Famer when you see one, and they more than meet the expectations.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] MLB wild-card preview: Series predictions, X-factors and more for Red Sox-Yankees, Cubs-Padres, Phillies-Braves and White Sox-Astros
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz
item.description: The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical. Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins. AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves Projected starters (all times ET) Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luza
item.content:encoded:
The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical.
Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins.
AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD
No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luzardo (PHI) vs. Chris Sale (ATL)
Game 2, 2 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL)
Game 3, TBD*: Aaron Nola (or Zack Wheeler on four days' rest) (PHI) vs. Grant Holmes (ATL)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Phillies: It was a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde type of season for the Phillies, to say the least. For the second time in five seasons, an in-season managerial firing was needed to light a fire under an underperforming veteran roster that appeared to be letting their window close. But the Phillies, like they've done before, found a way to get themselves going on the back of their starting rotation. The Phillies didn't make it easy on themselves in September, going 10-14 down the stretch and needing to win their regular-season finale against the Rays to punch their ticket to the postseason. But now that they're in, this veteran group will look to show that they're better than the past month suggests.
Braves: It was a reassuring year in Atlanta, a much-needed reminder that no, this era of Braves baseball was not over after their disastrous, postseason-less 2025. A change in manager, from the now-retired Brian Snitker to the endearingly pugnacious Walt Weiss, set the tone. As did a major refresh of Atlanta's coaching staff. That turnover, in contrast with the continuity on the roster, proved crucial as Atlanta waltzed to its first division title since 2023.
Big campaigns from metronomic first baseman Matt Olson and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin shocked nobody. The same was true for ace Chris Sale, certain to be voted an NL Cy Young finalist. But few would've predicted Michael Harris II leading the team in bWAR with a dynamic, consistent offensive season. Role players such as Mauricio Dubón, Mike Yastrzemski and Dominic Smith all delivered critical production to help offset underwhelming seasons from the likes of Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley.
Ronald Acuña Jr., that wonderfully mercurial burst of baseballing light, might've fit into that last group if not for an otherworldly September in which he clocked seven homers with a .950 OPS. That renaissance continuing into October would be a game-changer for the Braves, whose 2021 title came with Acuña sidelined.
X-factors
Phillies: Trea Turner
The regular season wasn't kind to shortstop Trea Turner, who recorded the worst season of his career. But the thing about the postseason is that it allows players who have not yet written the final story on their season to become heroes. And if the Phillies want to move past Atlanta and reach the NLDS for the fifth straight year, Turner finding his rhythm would be a welcomed sight for the team's offense. Turner has a .733 OPS off Sale in 25 career at-bats and a very respectable .863 OPS off Mahle in 25 career at-bats.
Braves: Tyler Mahle
Chris Sale is going to start Game 1 for Atlanta, and he's probably going to be pretty good. That feels as bankable as anything in our topsy-turvy world. But Mahle, set to throw Game 2, has been one of the game's most reliable starters since he joined the Braves from a zip-less San Francisco team at the deadline. The veteran righty posted a 1.99 ERA with Atlanta, allowing one earned or fewer in seven of his nine starts.
Mahle's most recent start, however, was a relative stinker. He surrendered five runs and struck out just four at home against an undermanned Reds lineup. And the underlying metrics, it should be said, are a bit more skeptical about Mahle's prospects. That's understandable. He doesn't throw that hard or strike out oodles of hitters. He hasn't conjured more swing-and-miss or meaningfully lowered opponents' hard-hit rate as a Brave. And yet, Mahle has found a way to find outs. Whether he can do so against Philly's bats will be huge.
How they win
Phillies: Can any team in baseball go toe-to-toe with Philly's starting rotation? With the quartet of Wheeler, Sánchez, Luzardo and Nola, the Phillies should have the advantage in a three-, five- or seven-game series. So while their offense is more of a wild card (pun intended), this team should be able to count on its starter giving them a chance to win every time out. And if that foursome gets hot, it's not outlandish to believe they could carry Philly on another deep postseason run.
Braves: It has been a restful week for the Braves, who were able to sit back, relax and line up their starting rotation for this wild-card series. The same cannot be said for Philly, which needed every last out to clinch on the regular season's final day. For the Phillies, the sense of exhaustion is real and gives Atlanta a legitimate advantage.
But it all starts with Sale. If he cruises like he's capable of in Game 1, that puts Atlanta in the catbird seat. Only one team in the current playoff format (the 2025 Yankees) came back to win a wild-card series after losing the first game.
Series prediction: Braves in 3
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 3 Houston Astros
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 5 p.m. ET Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): David Sandlin (CWS) vs. Peter Lambert (HOU)
Game 2 5 p.m. ET Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU)
Game 3, TBD*: Davis Martin (CWS) vs. Hayden Wesneski (HOU)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
White Sox: The White Sox have been easily one of the best stories of the 2026 regular season, reaching the postseason for the first time since 2021. Chicago became the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason following three consecutive 100-loss seasons, capturing the third AL wild-card spot. The offense, led by first-time All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami, was the driving force behind the Sox's success. Chicago finished the season with a top-five offense in MLB.
The fact that the White Sox didn't win the AL Central might come as a disappointment, considering they were in first place for the majority of the second half. Still, it's undeniable that any result that puts them in the playoffs is a huge victory for the organization and a fan base that has been waiting for competitive baseball.
Astros: For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past. Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason. But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday.
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
X-factors
White Sox: Munetaka Murakami
Munetaka Murakami is a game-changer, and his presence in the White Sox's lineup is a huge advantage in the postseason. The White Sox's rookie slugger burst onto the scene in 2026, hitting 35 home runs and providing instant impact in his first season after coming over from Japan. But following a midseason hamstring injury, the league seemed to adjust to him; Murakami finished with a slashline of .184/.328/.423 and 11 homers since Aug 1. Still, he has the type of power that can change a series by himself, and with three homers in the final week of the season, he appears to be coming out of his second-half slump. If Murakami has rediscovered his power stroke, it could change this series.
Astros: Isaac Paredes
Yordan Alvarez is currently the best hitter on earth. He cannot, under any circumstances, be allowed to dictate proceedings during this series. Chicago must make somebody else in Houston's mediocre lineup beat them. If there's a base open with Alvarez up, he should just stroll straight to first every time.
That puts a mountain of pressure on Paredes. The stocky third baseman has been hitting right behind Alvarez for most of the season and has, for the most part, showed well. He's a supremely weird hitter, one who rarely hits the ball hard or barrels it up. But Paredes doesn't whiff, doesn't punch out and has a preternatural knack for pulling the ball in the air. Expect him to come up multiple times in big spots with runners on.
How they win
White Sox: The White Sox's offense has carried them all season, and if they hope to advance to the ALDS against their division rival, they'll have to slug their way there. Vargas, Murakami and shortstop Colson Montgomery each finished the season with more than 30 longballs, and the Sox finished fifth in MLB in homers. For a team built to slug, Daikin Park in Houston isn't the worst environment to play in on the road. Chicago's power-packed lineup has shown that if they're hitting the ball out of the ballpark, offensively, they can play with anyone.
Astros: Houston desperately needs offensive contributions from someone besides Alvarez. Maybe it's the aforementioned Paredes or the en fuego Yainer Díaz. Perhaps Jose Altuve, 36 years old and in full decline, has one magical month left in his Hall of Fame career. But with such a tattered pitching staff, the Astros need to score to win. They also need to win the Hunter Brown start; he's far and away their best starter. They need a lot, frankly. And yet, much weirder October things have happened inside that East Texas thunderdome over the past decade.
Series prediction: Astros in 3
No. 5 Boston Red Sox vs. No. 4 New York Yankees
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 8 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Payton Tolle (BOS) vs. Cam Schlittler (NYY)
Game 2, 8 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY)
Game 3, TBD*: Ranger Suárez (BOS) vs. Gerrit Cole (NYY)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Red Sox: Odysseus would be proud. What a winding, bizarre and tumultuous road it has been for the Sox. Boston began the year like a snail on Unisom, posting a lackluster 9-17 record through April 24. That precipitated a dramatic, Red Wedding-style culling, in which manager Alex Cora and several other staff members were relieved of their duties. Extended injury list stints for the team's two most important pieces, outfielder Roman Anthony and 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, made a turnaround feel awfully unlikely. On July 24, the Sox lost a rubber match in Colorado and traveled home 14 games under .500. Their postseason odds wallowed around 10%.
Then, everything changed. It began with a home mop against the Yanks and fully kicked into gear when the Red Sox hit the road for a three-city swing the first week of July. They went 9-0 on that trip before winning six straight at home. That 15-game streak catapulted them back into contention and the good graces of an understandably unplugged fan base. Between July 3 and Aug. 7, the Sox went a ridiculous 32-5, trampolining from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over. Fenway was a zoo. Nothing could go wrong. Boston ballfans beamed once again.
The heater earned Cora's replacement, Chad Tracy, the full-time gig. It also afforded the Sox a relatively comfortable September. It's worth noting, though, that Boston has not played particularly crisply since cooling off from the volcanic run, with a 21-22 record since Aug. 8. Ultimately, their final numbers and standing in the American League are not shocking or unexpected, even though Boston's odyssey was wonky beyond comparison.
Yankees: For all the stress, the drama, the hand-wringing, for all the injuries and under-performance, 2026 was a relatively straightforward season in YankeeLand. A lot, it should be said, went wrong. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge has played just seven games since May. Giancarlo Stanton hasn't played since April. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón each missed about two months. Young players such as Anthony Volpe, Jasson Dominguez and Austin Wells regressed offensively. Gerrit Cole, coming back from Tommy John, didn't fully recapture his frontline best.
And yet, here the Yankees are, with 93 wins and in an identical place to where they finished last year. That's thanks to breakout campaigns from homegrown pieces such as Cam Schlittler (the AL Cy Young favorite) and Ben Rice (41 home runs and a .897 OPS). Closer David Bednar has been dynamite. Cody Bellinger has been a rock. Skipper Aaron Boone kept the train on the tracks. Three games at home against the Red Sox await. Beyond that looms an ALDS against a daunting division foe. We've been here before.
The largest difference, of course, is the uncertainty swirling around Judge. The Yankees' captain missed three months due to a rib problem, came back for a week, strained his calf and went back on the shelf. Boone says he's preparing for a wild-card round without Judge. Judge says he plans to play. What sort of magic this reduced version of Judge can conjure is easily the juiciest storyline ahead of this rivalry showdown. That said, this series, like this Yankees season, is probably going to be dictated by the pitchers.
X-factors
Red Sox: Roman Anthony
It has been an odd season for the 22-year-old, who missed last year's wild-card festivities due to injury. In March, Anthony was a late addition to Team USA's WBC roster. He shined on that grand stage, impressing his more established teammates and earning plaudits from a coaching staff of hardball lifers. That only ratcheted up the hype on a player expected to carry a franchise less than a year after he became legally permitted to drink a beer.
So when Anthony started slowly, disappointment bubbled. Then, on May 4, he tore a ligament in his finger; that kept him out of action until Aug. 30. A lot happened in the interim, most of which Anthony spent rehabbing at the team's complex in Florida. Since returning, he has looked promising, tantalizingly close to unleashing the full assortment of his talents upon the league. Now, with Willson Contreras banged up and either unavailable or restricted, the pressure returns to Anthony's young shoulders.
Yankees: Luis García Jr.
García was a curious character for the Yankees to shape their trade deadline around. Instead of acquiring a piece that filled an obvious void (righty stick with defensive value or versatility), GM Brian Cashman opted to add the most dynamic hitter possible. New York landed on García, who was in the midst of an offensive breakout under a new Washington Nationals regime.
For a month, that plan bore fruit, with the Dominican slugger posting an .846 OPS in August. But since then, the wheels have fallen off, with García's chase rate skyrocketing. His September OPS started with a 5. He has homered just twice since Aug. 26. He doesn't have an extra-base hit since Sept. 10. There's a chance, given Boston's bevy of southpaws and New York's DH surplus, that he doesn't start every game. But García will get his chances, and whether he comes up big might swing the series.
How they win
Red Sox: Boston's pitching staff is the only one in baseball that ranks in the top five in both home run rate and walk rate. That's a rare combo. Usually, throwing the ball in the strike zone more often leads to more hard contact. But these Red Sox hurlers, for whatever reason, have threaded that needle perfectly. No team in the league has allowed fewer homers. However, no team has hit more than the Yankees. Boston revitalized its season behind pitching and defense, keeping the scores low and the games close. Doing so here will give them the best chance of authoring an upset.
Yankees: No American League team can compete with New York's starting staff. But the Yankees need more than dominance from Schlittler, Fried and Cole. They need length. The bridge to Bednar is unsteady. So the longer the starters go, the rosier that path looks. Offensively, the Yankees need a big swing or two from their right-handed bats against Boston's left-handed arms. That could come from a banged-up Judge or Stanton. It could come from veteran southpaw-killer Paul Goldschmidt, trade-acquisition Heliot Ramos or rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. If it comes from the beleaguered Anthony Volpe, the tri-state area will lose its collective marbles. But somebody, anybody who stands on the right side of the batter's box has to make an impact.
Series prediction: Yankees in 3
No. 5 Chicago Cubs vs. No. 4 San Diego Padres
(all times ET)
Projected starters
Game 1, 10 p.m. Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): Shota Imanaga (CHC) vs. Michael King (SD)
Game 2, 10 p.m. Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Clay Holmes (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD)
Game 3, TBD*: Matthew Boyd (CHC) vs. Walker Buehler or Casey Mize or Robbie Ray (SD)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Cubs: It was Pete Crow-Armstrong's world, and the rest of us just lived in it. Chicago's 24-year-old center fielder went fully supersonic this year, cranking 45 homers, swiping 41 bags and delivering a .945 OPS with his typically elite outfield defense. He will win the NL MVP, and it might be unanimous. That performance shaped and guided and defined this Cubs' season, electrifying an offense that led baseball in OPS, K/BB rate and runs per game.
Alex Bregman's arrival via free agency, too, cannot be understated. He struggled mightily for the first few months, with his extended schneid at one point eliciting boos from a frustrated Wrigley crowd. But since July 12, Bregman leads all qualified National League hitters in OPS. His experience, comportment and leadership, by all accounts, have also had a meaningful impact on Crow-Armstrong.
But pitching woes, in both the rotation and the bullpen, kept Chicago from ever seriously threatening the Brewers for the NL Central title. The Cubs started the year on something of a roller coaster, with two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak before the calendar flipped to June. They'll enter October on something of an ice floe, with 15 runs scored in their final six contests.
Padres: San Diego has the best record in baseball since July 24. The day before, the Pads lost a rubber match in Atlanta to fall to three games under. 500. That pushed the club four games adrift of a wild-card spot, with the Cardinals, Pirates, Marlins, Nationals and Diamondbacks standing between them and a trip to October. That was the low-water mark for this team.
Since that date, the Padres have gone 41-18. They won five straight in late July, six straight in August and eight straight in September. They've lost thrice since Labor Day. The reason for the resurgence? Check out these numbers.
| Padres offensive ranks before and after July 24 | | |
| | Before | After |
| Runs/game | 4.14 (25th) | 4.95 (3rd) |
| AVG | .230 (28th) | .268 (2nd) |
| OBP | .307 (27th) | .339 (2nd) |
| SLG | .383 (27th) | .425 (2nd) |
| OPS | .689 (26th) | .764 (2nd) |
San Diego's offense went from bottom-five to top-five. Some of that is batted-ball luck and sequencing. A lot of it is Fernando Tatis Jr. turning back into a monster. Jackson Merrill had a similar rebirth. Ty France continued his bounce-back campaign. Xander Bogaerts shifted from unwatchable to capable. Unsung heroes such as Dustin Harris and Luis Rengifo got hot. The starting pitching did just enough. The game's best bullpen never stopped dominating. It's that unit, led by a cadre of flamethrowers in Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, that makes these Padres a particularly formidable October opponent.
X-factors
Cubs: Alex Bregman — specifically, his face
One week ago, Bregman was the victim of some very painful misfortune. A check-swing foul ball off the bat of Cubs first baseman Michael Busch struck Bregman in the face while he was standing in the on-deck circle. Blood dripped from below his left eye as he scurried down the dugout steps into the clubhouse. A trip to the hospital revealed multiple facial fractures. The incident kept Bregman out of the lineup until Friday, when he went 0-for-4 with a strikeout as Chicago's DH. He went 4-for-4 with two home runs and a walk in Sunday's season finale.
There's no doubt that Bregman, the textbook definition of a "grinder," will take the field in October. But at what level? He has been so integral to Chicago's lineup for the past few months that even a slightly reduced version of Bregman could unsettle things. Among active players, only his former Astros teammate Jose Altuve has taken more postseason plate appearances.
Padres: Fernando Tatis Jr.
Nothing is more meaningfully different about this year's Padres team compared to the one that went three and see-ya at Wrigley in 2025 than Fernando Tatis Jr.'s stunning offensive reemergence. Things didn't start so swimmingly this year for the swaggering outfielder, who needed 55 games to clock his first longball of this season. But since May 30, Tatis' .914 OPS ranks fourth in the NL, and his 4.9 fWAR ranks second in MLB behind only Crow-Armstrong.
This version of Tatis looks a lot like the one who took the baseball world by storm en route to finishing third in NL MVP in 2021. Will that brilliance show up in a small October sample? It usually has throughout the 27-year-old's career; he holds a 1.114 postseason OPS in 70 plate appearances. Tatis, though, has never advanced past the NLDS. Remember, he was in PED timeout when the Padres stampeded to the NLCS in 2022. Could this month be his path back to full-blown superstardom?
How they win
Cubs: The margins were razor thin when these teams lined up in the wild-card round last year, with a highlight reel of web gems from shortstop Dansby Swanson making the difference. Those games, oddly enough, were incredibly low-scoring, with Chicago snagging two 3-1 wins and San Diego edging out a 3-0 win. It's hard to imagine the Cubs and their underwhelming relief group winning that way again, particularly on the road. To advance, they'll need buckets of runs. With PCA, Bregman, Seiya Suzuki and Co., that's a real possibility.
Padres: The Padres' formula for success has been the same for the past few seasons: Shorten the game. San Diego realistically needs five innings from its starters. Then manager Craig Stammen gets to turn things over to the best relief core in baseball, led by southpaw Adrían Morejon and flamethrower Mason Miller. The Friars' starting pitching has gotten stronger as they've gotten healthy, so if Michael King in Game 1 and likely Nick Pivetta in Game 2 can each give San Diego 15 outs, the Padres have a good chance of making quick work of Chicago.

item.title: [MLB.com] Fresh off facial fractures, Bregman mashes 2 homers in 2nd game back

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG – Even without any postseason implications on the line on Sunday, Alex Bregman told Cubs manager Craig Counsell that he wanted to be in the starting lineup. The third baseman felt it was important for him to get more at-bats ahead of the playoffs.
And if there were any lingering questions about how Bregman was seeing the ball just a week removed from the fluke foul ball that resulted in multiple fractures in his left cheek, he offered an emphatic answer against the Red Sox. In only his second game back in the lineup, Bregman belted a pair of no-doubt homers in his first two at-bats at Tropicana Field.
Following two games on Friday at Fenway Park, where strong winds related to the Nor’easter hitting the region did a number on Chicago’s offense, the move to the neutral site gave the lineup a chance to hit reset. That was especially important for Bregman, who went 0-for-4 in his first game back in the opener of Friday’s twin bill.
Late Saturday night, Bregman went over video with Ben Martin, an assistant director of Major League development for the Cubs, at the team’s hotel. They found some issues with Bregman’s posture in his stance during Friday’s at-bats and went to work on correcting the issue. And on Sunday afternoon, Counsell received a text message from the third baseman.
“It just said, ‘LFG,’” Counsell said with a smirk. “I knew what it meant – I didn’t know what he was referring to. I thought he was referring to a football game or something like that. But he was like, ‘I found it and I’m ready. I feel good.’ And yeah, he did. He felt good. He was right.”
Bregman cracked a smile when asked about the text.
“[We were] trying to figure out what felt a little weird the first game back,” Bregman said. “I was kind of looking uphill and kind of [leaning] back. So I kind of got a little bit more into it, into a little bit more of an attacking posture today. It felt better.”
That is great news ahead of the upcoming National League Wild Card Series against the Padres.
“I’m not surprised that he’s performing when he’s back on the field,” Counsell said. “I’m surprised that he’s back on the field. Being back on the field is what I think we should all appreciate and admire.”
The only question right now is whether Counsell will put Bregman back at third base in the postseason, or keep him slotted in as the designated hitter for now. Bregman has been the DH in his first two games back in the fold, and Counsell hinted at staying in that mode as a way to minimize the risk of a setback.
Bregman took ground balls in a workout at Tropicana Field on Saturday’s off-day and will do so again during Monday’s workout at Petco Park in San Diego. Even so, Counsell is taking things day by day when it comes to weighing putting him back in the field.
“We’ll just kind of see how he feels every day,” Counsell said. “I think he’s improving every day, but he’s got multiple face fractures, and it’s been [a week]. So we’ll just see how he feels. One thing I’m thinking about is the risk of more exposure. I think his at-bats are the most important thing that we can get.”
Bregman said he is willing to do whatever Counsell asks of him.
“I want to play third, but I’ll do whatever it takes,” Bregman said.
Bregman went deep in the first and third inning – off a first-pitch sinker and then an 0-1 sweeper – and sent both pitches crashing into the left-field stands. Those were the 27th and 28th homers of the year for Bregman, who has been one of baseball’s best hitters in the second half. Entering the final game of the regular season, only Pete Crow-Armstrong (4.7), Fernando Tatis Jr. (3.7) and Elly De La Cruz (3.6) had a higher WAR (via FanGraphs) than Bregman (3.3) since the All-Star break.
Bregman added a single in the fifth inning, drew a walk in the seventh and added an RBI double in the ninth. When he reached base after those plate appearances, Bregman switched out one helmet (with an extended left earflap) for another that had a longer flap on each side to offer more protection.
“I felt like I was in a football helmet out there,” Bregman quipped.
Bregman was waiting on deck on Sept. 20 in Cincinnati when he was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch. Prior to that game, the Cubs’ third baseman had hit .298 with 19 homers, 18 doubles, 53 RBIs and a 1.000 OPS in his previous 60 games. His season OPS climbed to .801 from .670 in that span.
Beyond the homers, Bregman ended the year slashing .265/.355/.464 with 33 doubles, 76 walks, 92 runs scored, 93 RBIs and an .819 OPS in 155 games for the North Siders.
“The last two months of the season, I feel like that’s who I am as a player,” Bregman said. “I’m proud to know that no matter how big of a hole that I dug myself, I could find my way back out.”
